html:
The Lakota, or Teton Sioux, are the western division of the Sioux peoples, best known as the mounted bison hunters of the northern Plains. They are made up of seven bands, among them the Oglala, Sicangu (Brulé), Hunkpapa and Miniconjou.

In the 1600s they lived further east, around the upper Mississippi in Minnesota, beside their Yanktonai and Dakota kin. Pushed by the Ojibwe and pulled by the bison and the fur trade, they moved west across the Missouri in the 1700s, took up horses, and took the Black Hills from the Kiowa and the Cheyenne. By 1800 they were the strongest power on the northern Plains.

Against the United States they won Red Cloud's War of 1866 to 1868 and the Fort Laramie Treaty, which promised them the Black Hills. When gold was found there, war came again. Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse defeated Custer at the Little Bighorn in 1876, but the bands were forced onto reservations within a year. The killings at Wounded Knee in 1890 marked the end of armed resistance. Today the Lakota live mainly on reservations in South and North Dakota.
